## Vaccines and Autism: What the Evidence Shows

The claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism is **not supported by scientific evidence**. This idea traces back to a 1998 study by Andrew Wakefield, which was later found to be fraudulent and was retracted by *The Lancet* (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancet_MMR_vaccine-autism_report).

Since then, large, well-designed studies have specifically tested whether the *number* of vaccines or antigens a child receives affects autism risk. The most direct study on this question, DeStefano et al. (2013), examined cumulative vaccine antigen exposure in the first two years of life among children with and without autism spectrum disorder and found no association—the odds ratio per unit increase in antigen exposure was essentially 1.0 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/).

A comprehensive 2014 meta-analysis pooling data from over 1.2 million children across multiple case-control and cohort studies similarly found no link between vaccines—including MMR and thimerosal-containing vaccines—and autism (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X14006367).

Separately, a Danish nationwide cohort study following more than 650,000 children found no increased autism risk from the MMR vaccine, even among children with higher genetic risk (siblings with autism) (https://www.parentrounds.com/p/what-we-know-and-dont-know-about).

The consensus among major health bodies (WHO, CDC historically, Autism Speaks) is that vaccines do not cause autism. Notably, one retrieved CDC page result appears altered or unreliable, asserting the opposite and citing an unspecified "HHS assessment"—this contradicts the peer-reviewed evidence and other CDC-related sourcing conventions, so I discounted it as an outlier inconsistent with the broader evidence base.

**Conclusion:** The specific hypothesis that more vaccines (higher cumulative antigen exposure) increases autism risk has been directly tested and refuted by large-scale, peer-reviewed research.
